cls: Prostaglandin analog (ophthalmic, selective FP prostanoid receptor agonist)
pharm: Topical ophthalmic prostaglandin F2-alpha analog prodrug that is hydrolyzed in the cornea to its active free acid, lowering intraocular pressure by increasing uveoscleral aqueous outflow
quick: One drop in the affected eye(s) once daily in the evening
Potential fetal risk; use only if benefit justifies risk
Unknown if in human milk; weigh benefit against risk
Studied in renal impairment; no clinically relevant changes
Studied in hepatic impairment; no clinically relevant changes
Iris/eyelid pigmentation, eyelash changes, intraocular pressure
summary: Travoprost ophthalmic solution 0.004% is a prostaglandin analog eye drop used to reduce elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in patients with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension. The usual dose is one drop in the affected eye(s) once daily in the evening; more frequent dosing can reduce the IOP-lowering effect. It can cause gradual, often permanent increased brown pigmentation of the iris and increased pigmentation of the periorbital (eyelid) tissue and eyelashes, as well as longer, thicker, more numerous eyelashes. The most common adverse effect is conjunctival (ocular) hyperemia.
indications: Reduction of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in patients with open-angle glaucoma
Reduction of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in patients with ocular hypertension

dosage.d: One drop in the affected eye(s) once daily in the evening
dosage.n: Do not exceed once-daily dosing - more frequent use may reduce the IOP-lowering effect; IOP reduction begins about 2 hours after the first dose with maximum effect at about 12 hours

dosage.c: Adult on other topical eye drops
dosage.d: One drop once daily; administer different ophthalmic drugs at least 5 minutes apart
dosage.n: May be used concomitantly with other topical ophthalmic IOP-lowering products
Potential safety concern from increased pigmentation with long-term chronic use

admin: Instill one drop in the affected eye(s) once daily in the evening
If using more than one topical ophthalmic drug, separate each by at least 5 minutes
Remove contact lenses before instillation and reinsert 15 minutes afterward
Avoid letting the dropper tip touch the eye, surrounding structures, fingers, or any surface to prevent contamination
After opening, the bottle may be used until the expiration date printed on it
moa: Travoprost free acid is a selective FP prostanoid receptor agonist (a prostaglandin F analog) that is believed to reduce intraocular pressure by increasing uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor; the exact mechanism is not fully known.

relative: Active intraocular inflammation (e.g., uveitis) - may be exacerbated
Aphakia, pseudophakia with a torn posterior lens capsule, or other risk factors for macular edema
Not evaluated for angle-closure, inflammatory, or neovascular glaucoma
monitor: Iris, periorbital (eyelid), and eyelash pigmentation changes
Signs of intraocular inflammation or macular edema
Signs of bacterial keratitis (especially with corneal disease or epithelial disruption)

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. In animal reproduction studies, subcutaneous travoprost during organogenesis produced embryo-fetal lethality, spontaneous abortion, and premature delivery at potentially clinically relevant doses, and was teratogenic in rats at higher exposures. Travoprost should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus, and pregnant women should be advised of a potential risk.
lact: There are no data on the effects of travoprost on the breastfed child or on milk production, and it is not known whether travoprost is present in human milk after ophthalmic use; in lactating rats radiolabeled travoprost or its metabolites were excreted in milk after subcutaneous dosing. Weigh the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's clinical need for travoprost and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child.
renal: Travoprost ophthalmic solution has been studied in patients with renal impairment, with no clinically relevant changes in hematology, blood chemistry, or urinalysis observed. No dose adjustment is described.
hepatic: Travoprost ophthalmic solution has been studied in patients with hepatic impairment, with no clinically relevant changes in hematology, blood chemistry, or urinalysis observed. No dose adjustment is described.

moderate: Other topical ophthalmic drugs - administer at least 5 minutes apart to avoid washout
interactions.diagnostics: Remove contact lenses before instillation and reinsert after 15 minutes

common: Ocular (conjunctival) hyperemia (reported in 30% to 50% of patients)
Decreased visual acuity, eye discomfort, foreign body sensation, eye pain, ocular pruritus (5% to 10%)
serious: Macular edema, including cystoid macular edema
Bacterial keratitis from contaminated multiple-dose containers
rare: Iris discoloration, keratitis, blepharitis, conjunctivitis, corneal staining, subconjunctival hemorrhage, dry eye, photophobia (1% to 4%)
Periorbital and lid changes including deepening of the eyelid sulcus (postmarketing)
Systemic: arrhythmia, tachycardia, epistaxis, vomiting, insomnia (postmarketing)
emergency: Sudden eye pain, marked redness, or vision loss (possible severe ocular reaction or infection)

monitoring: Iris, periorbital (eyelid), and eyelash pigmentation - examine regularly if iris pigmentation increases
Signs of intraocular inflammation or macular edema
Signs of ocular infection (bacterial keratitis), particularly with corneal disease
counsel: Use one drop in the affected eye(s) once daily in the evening; do not use more often than directed
Be aware travoprost can cause a gradual, likely permanent increase in brown iris pigmentation and possible eyelid skin darkening (eyelid darkening may be reversible)
Eyelashes and fine facial hair may become longer, thicker, more numerous, or differ between eyes; these changes are usually reversible after stopping
Do not let the dropper tip touch your eye, fingers, or any surface, to avoid contaminating the solution and causing eye infection
Remove contact lenses before each dose and reinsert them 15 minutes later
If using other eye drops, wait at least 5 minutes between them
Seek your doctor's advice promptly for eye injury, infection, eye surgery, or new eye reactions such as conjunctivitis or eyelid reactions
pk: IOP reduction begins about 2 hours after the first dose
Maximum IOP-lowering effect at about 12 hours; plasma Cmax of free acid reached within about 30 minutes
Plasma half-life of the free acid about 45 minutes
Once-daily dosing maintains IOP control; no significant systemic accumulation
Store at 2-25 C (36-77 F); after opening, use until the expiration date on the bottle
pearls: Dose in the EVENING - more frequent than once-daily dosing can paradoxically reduce the IOP-lowering effect
Iris pigmentation change is due to increased melanin in existing melanocytes, not more melanocytes, and is likely permanent; eyelid and eyelash changes are often reversible
Most common adverse effect is conjunctival/ocular hyperemia (30% to 50%); up to 3% discontinue because of it
Use with caution in aphakic or pseudophakic eyes with a torn posterior capsule and in those at risk for macular edema
Not recommended under 16 years of age because of long-term pigmentation safety concerns
missed: If you miss an evening dose, skip it and resume your regular once-daily schedule with the next evening dose. Do not use extra drops to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: An ocular overdose of travoprost is not likely to cause serious harm; if too much is instilled, flush the eye(s) with lukewarm water. Treat symptomatically. Because systemic absorption is minimal, systemic overdose effects are unlikely.
